changes: Replace the Netherlands electric bike and China pork examples in the questions with Australian or Victorian market examples, since the course is for students in Victoria.
match.reason: The bank point teaches the same idea at the right depth, including the rule that demand shifts move price and quantity together while supply shifts move them oppositely, but its examples are foreign and should be localised for a Victorian VCE course.

confirm.reason: The closest bank point, e-equilibrium, also covers what equilibrium is and how a market clears, so it is broader than this point, which teaches only how shifts in demand or supply change the equilibrium.

rejected.title: Changes in equilibrium
card: A market is in equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A shift in demand or supply breaks that balance, and the market settles at a new equilibrium price and quantity.
Demand shifts
An increase in demand shifts the curve right, so price and quantity both rise. A decrease in demand shifts it left, so price and quantity both fall.
Supply shifts
An increase in supply shifts the curve right, so price falls and quantity rises. A decrease in supply shifts it left, so price rises and quantity falls.
First decide which curve shifted and which way. A change that affects buyers shifts demand, and a change that affects sellers shifts supply. Then read off the new price and quantity.
rejected.remember: Demand shifts move price and quantity the same way. Supply shifts move them in opposite ways.

a.q: Heavy rain destroys part of the tomato crop in Victoria, and nothing else changes. What happens in the tomato market?
a.why: The crop loss affects sellers and decreases supply, so the supply curve shifts left. Price rises and the quantity traded falls. Price and quantity do not both rise, because that happens when demand increases.
a.clue: Does the rain affect buyers or sellers?

b.q: Incomes rise across Geelong, and nothing else changes. What happens in the market for restaurant meals there?
b.why: Higher incomes let buyers spend more, which increases demand for restaurant meals, so the demand curve shifts right. Price and quantity both rise. Price would fall only with an increase in supply or a decrease in demand, and neither happened here.
b.clue: Start by asking whose plans a change in income affects.

a.q: Heavy rain destroys part of the tomato crop in Victoria, and nothing else changes. What happens in the tomato market?
a.why: The crop loss decreases supply, so the supply curve shifts left. Price rises and the quantity traded falls. Price and quantity do not both rise, because that happens only when demand increases.
a.clue: Which curve shifted, and which way?

b.q: Incomes rise across Geelong, and nothing else changes. What happens in the market for restaurant meals there?
b.why: Higher incomes increase demand for restaurant meals, so the demand curve shifts right. Price and quantity both rise. Price does not fall, because falling price comes with an increase in supply.
b.clue: Demand moves price and quantity the same way.

problems.detail: The why says a falling price 'comes with an increase in supply', but a decrease in demand also lowers price. It should say that a falling price here would need an increase in supply or a decrease in demand, neither of which happened.

The clue 'Demand moves price and quantity the same way' tells the student that demand is the curve that shifted, which is the step the question is testing. That leaves only two options, so the clue gives away much of the answer.

check.summary: Both answers are clear and correct. The why for (b) wrongly says a falling price comes only from an increase in supply (a fall in demand also lowers price), and the clue for (b) gives away which curve shifted.

problems.detail: "A change that affects buyers shifts demand, and a change that affects sellers shifts supply" is too broad. A change in the good's own price affects both buyers and sellers, yet it causes a movement along the curves, not a shift. Limit the rule to non-price factors, for example "a change in something other than the price".
